1.title: Cover
1.summary: Front cover of 'Shoqëria dhe Mjedisi 4' (Society and Environment 4, for grade four of primary school) with the three authors' names. The illustration shows a globe, a closed book, scales of justice, a pencil and large green leaves on a purple table.

2.title: Blank page
2.summary: Empty page with no text or pictures (inside of the cover).

3.title: Contents (part 1)
3.summary: First page of the table of contents. It lists the foreword, 'I am growing up' and the units on cooperation with others, rights and responsibilities, understanding/solidarity/empathy, shared decision-making, and 'The place where I live' (Kosovo), with page numbers.

4.title: Contents (part 2)
4.summary: Second page of the table of contents. It lists the units on life in Kosovo then and now, traditions and heritage, the country's resources and heritage, and the environment, ending with a game and the references.

5.title: Foreword
5.summary: A letter from the authors to the pupils explaining what the grade-4 book covers: social groups and cooperation, rights and institutions, cultural diversity and tolerance, decision-making, Kosovo and its regions and neighbours, the economy, hygiene, natural resources and recycling. Text only; no story.

6.title: I Am Growing Up
6.summary: Linda, a fourth-grader, tells how she has grown up: every morning she washes, tidies her room and dresses for the season, eats healthy food on time, does her homework, practises ballet, takes foreign-language courses, behaves well in public, helps her parents cook and set the table, plays with friends and reads in bed before sleep. Pictures would illustrate a girl's daily routines and hobbies (ballet, tidying, cooking, reading).

7.title: I Am Growing Up (questions and table)
7.summary: Questions about why Linda's parents say she has grown, and a table where the pupil compares themself with Linda (habits, food, clothes, shoes, talent, foreign language, housework, reading, behaviour, following rules). An information box explains that people grow and change physically (height, weight) and mentally (habits, telling right from wrong, learning) when surrounded by loving adults.

8.title: Our Community
8.summary: Unit: Links and cooperation with others. People living in a neighbourhood are a community: they are responsible for their neighbours and decide together on changes for everyone's good. In the situation, the neighbourhood has an empty, unbuilt plot and all the residents are thinking about what to use it for; the pupil is asked for their own idea. A box defines 'community'.

9.title: Our Community (illustration)
9.summary: Full-page picture for the community lesson: a pink three-storey apartment house with a red roof, neighbours at every window (one hanging laundry on a balcony), and on the street in front children riding a long tandem bicycle, a mother and daughter walking a dog, two girls hugging, children on a bench and a collie. It shows neighbours sharing one living space.

10.title: Social Groups
10.summary: Unit: Links and cooperation with others. Bora, a fourth-grader living in Prishtina with her parents and older brother, belongs to her school's dance group and recitation group, while her brother is in the football group and the painting group. The page teaches that a social group is people with shared ideas, goals or activities, and that one person belongs to many groups at once (family, class, neighbourhood, sports or music group).

11.title: Social Groups (illustration)
11.summary: Full-page pictures for the social-groups lesson: three children dancing happily with music notes around them (Bora's dance group), and a boy in football kit kicking a ball in front of a goal (her brother's football group).

12.title: Our Common Good
12.summary: Unit: Links and cooperation with others. During the cold end-of-year holidays, schoolchildren organise a charity action called 'We give little pieces of happiness': each brings what they can for children in need - clothes they no longer wear, scarves, gloves, notebooks, school supplies, hygiene products - and they talk about the gifts they prepared. The page teaches humanism: voluntary work, care and help for others' well-being.

13.title: Together We Succeed
13.summary: Unit: Links and cooperation with others. At the end of August, Lisi tidies his bedroom before starting fourth grade; he likes reusing and recycling and does not know what to do with his treasured first books. His parents suggest collecting books from classmates too and creating a class library where children exchange books. The page teaches teamwork: people with a shared goal dividing tasks equally.

14.title: Activity 1: Volunteer Work Unites Us
14.summary: Unit: Links and cooperation with others. A class activity: the class splits into two groups - the first bakes sweets/cakes at home, the second makes decorated greeting cards from recycled materials. They sell them at a stand in the school and use the money to buy equipment for pupils of another school in need. Pictures show the sweets and the handmade cards.

15.title: My Rights and Responsibilities
15.summary: Unit: Everyone has rights and responsibilities. In the classroom during break, pupils gather and talk; the teacher reminds them not to make noise or run around because they could disturb or hurt each other. She explains that they have the right to education but also the responsibility to know and respect school rules and to study hard.

16.title: My Rights and Responsibilities (situation 2)
16.summary: A girl's family watches television together in the evening; she is inattentive during the news, but her mother advises her to listen because the information can affect her life. One night a report about infectious diseases teaches her to keep physical distance from her friends. The picture would show a family watching the TV news.

17.title: My Rights and Responsibilities (questions and info)
17.summary: Questions about the mother's advice, why information matters and how to protect oneself from infectious diseases. The information box explains the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, civil/political versus social/economic/cultural rights, and the 54-article Convention on the Rights of the Child (20 November 1989), stressing that rights and responsibilities go together.

18.title: Institutions That Protect Us
18.summary: A reminder from grade 3 of whom to phone in an emergency - police, ambulance/emergency service, firefighters (three pictures). In the situation, a nurse comes to the classroom to check the children's hygiene and health, on behalf of the Institute of Public Health. Pupils then role-play doctor and patient.

19.title: Institutions That Protect Us (situation 2)
19.summary: In a noisy city, a traffic police officer stops the cars and stands at the zebra crossing (white lines) at the times children enter and leave school, so they cross safely. The information box says the state protects human rights through its institutions and mentions the United Nations, the OSCE and the Ombudsperson.

20.title: Activity 2: Visit to a Health Centre
20.summary: A picture-discussion page with three illustrations: a doctor listening to a girl's chest with a stethoscope on an examination bed, a nurse/doctor measuring a boy's height on a scale, and a dentist in a mask examining a boy in a dental chair. Pupils say what they see, which right each picture relates to (health care) and whether they know their family doctor.

21.title: Activity 2: Visit to a Health Centre (continued)
21.summary: Questions about visiting the family doctor and following medical advice, plus an explanation that health care means preventing, treating and curing illness and that doctors must help everyone equally and respect patients' rights. Tips: know preventive measures, get all vaccinations, have a health booklet/card, go for regular check-ups. A picture would show children with a family doctor.

22.title: We Respect Cultural Diversity
22.summary: Unit: Understanding, solidarity, empathy and respect. The narrator's older sister has studied and worked in Turkey for three years and shares a dormitory with a Chinese, a Turkish and an Iranian girl; she tells the family about their cultures, especially Chinese greetings and eating habits. Next time she will bring her Chinese friend, so the family must cook rice the Chinese way and not eat it with forks (chopsticks).

23.title: We Respect Cultural Diversity (situation 2)
23.summary: Flower colours mean different things in different cultures: yellow is joy, but courage in Japan and mourning in Egypt; white is purity in the West but mourning and sadness in China and Japan; red is good luck in China but danger in the West; tulips are positive everywhere. Classmates give a bouquet to their classmate Lu, whose family runs a business in Prishtina, for his birthday, but the (white) flowers upset him instead of pleasing him. The box explains national culture and cultural diversity.

24.title: I Feel Equal
24.summary: Besa, a girl in a wheelchair, watches her classmates play basketball on the court with shining eyes; she is their most faithful fan. The basketball coach announces he has planned something special for her (pupils continue the story - e.g. including her in the game). Teaches inclusion of children with disabilities; the picture shows a girl in a wheelchair at a basketball court.

25.title: I Feel Equal (situation 2)
25.summary: Nora wonders how to help her desk-mate, a boy who struggles with maths and is often corrected by the teacher for getting exercises wrong; pupils continue the story. The information box says children with disabilities or learning difficulties must get the same opportunities, be included in school and community, and be neither despised nor pitied.

26.title: A Different Opinion
26.summary: The Society and Environment teacher opens the lesson by asking whether it is better to watch a film or read a novel. Andi and Tea say the film is easier to remember and saves time; Trina and Redon say the book leaves room for imagination and creativity. Everyone joins the discussion, giving different opinions while waiting their turn to speak.

27.title: A Different Opinion (situation 2)
27.summary: The narrator's friend Vjosa moved to Germany with her family; when she comes back for the summer the narrator hardly recognises her because she is wearing very wide trousers that look like a dress. It shows that dress and behaviour differ between places. The box says having a different opinion is natural and should be seen as a value, not an obstacle.

28.title: Religious Diversity in Our Country
28.summary: At midday a child hears both the call from a mosque's minaret and the bells of a church; the parents take the child for a walk to a place where the mosque and the church stand side by side and explain religious diversity and respect for everyone's faith. The photos show religious buildings in Ferizaj (mosque and church next to each other), Prishtina in 1930, and Gjakova.

29.title: Religious Diversity in Our Country (situation 2)
29.summary: A history lesson about periods 'before Christ' reminds a child of Christmas films with Santa Claus (the New Year's Old Man) and his sack of presents, and of the gifts received from relatives for Bajram (Eid) and other holidays. The box explains religious coexistence: different faith groups living together in peace, with the school teaching tolerance.

30.title: Values
30.summary: The narrator and Dritan hurry to the puppet theatre to be on time, leaving Dritan's little sister behind, dragging her feet and crying. At the theatre door a bent but energetic old man arrives carrying the little girl in his arms, and the two boys feel guilty. Teaches care for younger siblings; the picture shows the old man bringing the small girl to the boys at the theatre.

31.title: Values (situation 2)
31.summary: During distance (online) learning a classmate, Besmir, has no phone to follow lessons; the narrator remembers that his grandmother was given a phone and thinks Besmir needs it more (pupils finish the story - lending/giving him the phone). The box says different people have different needs - a deaf or blind person, a struggling pupil, a younger sibling - and helping them shows our true values.

32.title: Solidarity - A Human Value
32.summary: A lonely old man lives in the children's alley and often watches them play in front of his wooden gate as their only spectator. He has not been seen for weeks, and one afternoon the children see a nurse coming out of his wooden door (he is ill). Pupils continue the story about how to help sick people who live alone.

33.title: Solidarity - A Human Value (situation 2)
33.summary: In 2020 the coronavirus pandemic frightened the whole world, and people showed humanity and solidarity during lockdowns by helping to save those at risk. The box defines solidarity as supporting people in hard moments and acting for the good of others. Pictures would show pandemic-time help (masks, medical staff, delivering food to neighbours).

34.title: Equality for All
34.summary: The school is holding a football championship and children volunteer for the team; they often play football together in their free time, but Blerta, a girl, is not included in the school team. Pupils continue the story and find a fair solution for her. Teaches equal chances for girls and boys in sport.

35.title: Equality for All (situation 2)
35.summary: A child says they never felt unequal to boys or girls, because at home the parents never divided chores into 'boys' work' and 'girls' work' and cared for all the children alike. The box explains equality before the law, gender equality, preventing gender-based violence, and teachers treating all pupils with respect. A picture would show brothers and sisters sharing housework.

36.title: Tolerance and Friendship
36.summary: Situation 1: Vjosa, a fourth-grader with poor eyesight, lacks the equipment for online lessons; her classmate Shpat persuades his older brother (who has the same difficulty and just got a new reading device) to give his old device, which enlarges letters on the screen, to Vjosa. Situation 2: a desk-mate arrives late, sad and tired, and when the girl Jeta pokes him from behind with a pen he shouts 'Don't tease me!'.

37.title: Tolerance and Friendship (questions and tips)
37.summary: Questions about whether Jeta's poking and the boy's reaction were right, and a debate on 'Good friends are tolerant'. The box defines tolerance (accepting others without prejudice) and friendship (love, trust, honesty, respect), followed by five tips on what tolerance teaches: valuing people who are different, accepting other opinions, building bridges, avoiding quarrels.

38.title: We Support Each Other
38.summary: In the narrator's family everyone contributes. The older brother works at a TV station and is paid by the hour; last month he was busy painting the house, barely earned anything and could not buy his younger sibling the usual favourite chocolates, which embarrassed him. In the evening the mother comes home with chocolates and a big cake, saying 'These are from me today'.

39.title: We Support Each Other (situation 2)
39.summary: Genti is a very good football player whose school team often wins, but in the next championship the team has trouble organising its play, so he thinks of asking his childhood friend, an equally good player, to join them. The box says individuals need each other's support in family, school and community, and shared activities strengthen friendship.

40.title: With Mind and Heart for People
40.summary: Ten-year-old Besmir's optic nerves are completely damaged by an eye disease and he risks being left out of school. An educational institution hires a special teacher for him and provides all the assistive equipment so he does not feel different from his peers; his parents are deeply grateful. The picture would show a boy with visual impairment learning with a support teacher.

41.title: With Mind and Heart for People (situation 2)
41.summary: Mother Teresa is given as the model of love and support for people. Everyone helps as they can: children help the elderly near them, doctors help patients, teachers help children including those with difficulties, and friends help each other. The box defines empathy as understanding other people's feelings.

42.title: Activity 3: How to Be Good Citizens?
42.summary: A picture-discussion page: five children sit around a round table planning a charity activity, with thought bubbles showing a box of toys, a pile of folded clothes and a stack of books (things to collect and donate). Pupils discuss how the children will organise it, whose help to ask for, and then split into working groups so the whole class takes part.

43.title: Activity 3: How to Be Good Citizens? (steps)
43.summary: Steps for the group activity: choose the theme, explain why taking part matters, assign responsibilities, pick the place and time, consider children's needs, find the best solutions, involve everyone and draw conclusions. The box says children have the right to speak and participate, and that acting to help the community makes someone a good citizen.

44.title: I Respect the Other's Opinion
44.summary: Unit: Different opinions, shared decisions. Situation 1: the teacher proposes a class trip to a historical place; Dritan wants Kruja (Skanderbeg's history, the museum, the old streets) while Blerta, who has been there, prefers Prizren (the League of Prizren). Situation 2: a family discusses dividing housework and helping the grandparents, but the older brother works almost all day and is often absent from the discussions.

45.title: I Respect the Other's Opinion (questions and info)
45.summary: Questions on how to hear the busy older brother's opinion and include him in family discussions. The box explains that people have different opinions and that listening calmly and tolerantly prevents conflict; respect for others' opinions is the basis of understanding and a culture of dialogue.

46.title: Steps of Decision-Making
46.summary: Situation 1: children take part in decisions at school - they propose and plan activities and divide themselves into groups by role. Situation 2: the school is being rebuilt and the project drawing is displayed on the front of the building; the pupils notice it has no gym or games hall, talk to the physical-education teacher, and he tells them to send a written request to the school management.

47.title: Steps of Decision-Making (questions and steps)
47.summary: Pupils write a request proposing a school gym. The box explains decision-making as discussion and compromise under agreed rules, then lists the steps: state clearly what is being decided, present facts, offer solutions, weigh pros and cons, seek agreement, and if none is reached vote - the option with most votes wins.

48.title: Let's Decide Together
48.summary: At the start of each school year there is a parents' meeting where the parents' council is elected; a pupil is curious whether parents follow the same election rules the pupils use. Pupils act out electing their class president. The picture would show a parents' meeting or a classroom vote.

49.title: Let's Decide Together (situation 2)
49.summary: A new girl, Jeta, has joined the class from another town; one day she arrives late and upset, and the class learns she lives with and looks after her grandmother because her parents had to go abroad for work. Pupils discuss how to help her. The box explains class presidents, the school council and parent representatives, followed by a two-group task on reaching (or failing to reach) a class decision.

50.title: In the Family We Decide Together
50.summary: Situation 1: the mother gets a good job offer that may mean moving to another town; the child overhears the parents' dilemma and is unhappy about leaving friends. Situation 2: for the family's end-of-year gift tradition the children plan a surprise for their mum - each brother and sister writes a gift idea on a piece of paper, and the little brother asks how they will decide (voting).

51.title: In the Family We Decide Together (info and tips)
51.summary: Questions on how the children will choose the mother's gift. The box says family members have rights and responsibilities and that children should have age-appropriate duties and express opinions freely (Convention on the Rights of the Child). Tips: ask family for advice, keep a calendar of family celebrations, listen carefully, respect others' opinions, choose words well.

52.title: In Our Community
52.summary: At a bus stop a boy with a bicycle tries to board the bus, but a sign by the door says bicycles and motor vehicles are not allowed; an elderly man tells him he must follow the rule, a decision accepted by everyone. The narrator wonders whether children in wheelchairs/pushchairs are allowed on the bus. Teaches following community rules.

53.title: In Our Community (situation 2)
53.summary: Classrooms are hard to heat; the pupils think of heaters or air conditioners, but the teacher says energy costs would rise, so they plan a meeting with municipality representatives and write a request. The box explains that a decision is a choice between alternatives, must not harm others, and that citizens take part in decision-making.

54.title: Institutions and Decisions
54.summary: For days the family's flat has had no drinking water and the water company gave no notice. The father asks the mother whether the contract mentions interruptions for technical reasons, and the child, hearing about service contracts for the first time, feels grown up. Pupils read a utility contract with their parents.

55.title: Institutions and Decisions (situation 2)
55.summary: Through elections citizens choose members of parliament, and the members of parliament elect the president as a unifying figure. The box explains unwritten social rules versus binding laws, central and local institutions, voting from age 18, and that parliament passes laws and elects the government and president. Pictures would show voting/ballot box and parliament.

56.title: Decision-Making Then and Now
56.summary: At home Bledi tells his father that children's voices should be heard in family decisions. His father answers that things have changed: they do ask the children, whereas when he was a boy Bledi's grandfather, as head of the family, decided everything alone - and today the grandfather is happy to hear his grandchildren speak freely. The box says decisions are now made through group discussion and the majority's opinion.

57.title: Decision-Making Then and Now (illustration)
57.summary: Full-page picture for the lesson: a boy (Bledi) and his father sitting on a sofa in a living room with bookshelves, a coffee table and a window, talking and smiling. It illustrates their conversation about how family decisions were made in the past and today.

58.title: Activity 4: How to Make the Right Decision?
58.summary: Three pictures with captions: children discussing around a table ('To discuss means to express your opinion alongside the other's'), the same group with one child presenting ('Base your opinions on arguments'), and four pupils with backpacks, one raising a hand ('Listen carefully when others speak'). The box says good decisions put the common good first and that all opinions should be heard and argued.

59.title: Visit to a Law Office
59.summary: Four pictures with captions about legal professions: the judge examines facts, hears witnesses and decides; the prosecutor presents the facts against the accused; the notary certifies that documents are genuine; the lawyer defends the accused by interpreting the laws. Pupils talk about their visit to a law office; the box describes a fair, transparent justice system based on Kosovo's laws.

60.title: Kosovo - My Homeland
60.summary: Unit: The place where I live. The teacher asks pupils to write what they know about Kosovo; they write poems and hold a class contest, and Mali's poem 'Kosova' wins and is sent to an editorial office for publication. The poem praises Kosovo's Sharr mountains, the hero Adem Jashari, brave fighters and mothers, green mountains, the Constitution and the law. The box explains 'homeland' and the three branches of power: Parliament, Government, Judiciary.

61.title: Independence of Kosovo
61.summary: Six-year-old Kledi's family is packing suitcases for a holiday in England, his first flight. Looking at his passport he asks about the emblem on it, and his father explains that every state has a flag, a coat of arms and an anthem, that Kosovo declared independence on 17 February 2008, and that the six stars on the flag stand for the peoples living in Kosovo. Pictures: family packing, a Kosovo passport, the flag and coat of arms.

62.title: Independence of Kosovo (questions and symbols)
62.summary: Questions about Independence Day and the state symbols; pupils stand and sing the anthem. The box describes 17 February 2008 as the main national holiday and the symbols: the blue flag with a yellow map of Kosovo and six white stars for the six ethnic communities, the coat of arms, and the anthem played at state ceremonies and sports events.

63.title: Regions of Kosovo
63.summary: Classmates Luna and Lisi study at Lisi's home, where his mother, geography teacher Lirika, teaches through play with a map of Kosovo coloured blue and yellow for the two regions: the Kosovo Plain and the Dukagjin Plain. She places name labels for the seven regional centres - Gjakova, Peja, Prizren in Dukagjin; Ferizaj, Gjilan, Mitrovica, Prishtina in the Kosovo Plain - with the capital Prishtina in red. The page shows this map.

64.title: Regions of Kosovo (landmarks)
64.summary: Questions about the regions, then a chart of landmarks of each regional centre: Peja - Rugova Gorge and the source of the White Drin; Gjakova - Çabrat Hill and the Erenik and Krena rivers; Prizren - the League of Prizren building and the Sharr mountains; Ferizaj - the US Army camp; Gjilan - the medieval fortress of Artana (Novobërda); Mitrovica - the Trepça mine; Prishtina - the National Library, National Museum, Ethnographic Museum and University. Pupils research landmarks of their own region.

65.title: Communities and Their Characteristics
65.summary: Klea's grandmother loves embroidery and has embroidered flowers on Klea's dresses and sweaters; she decides to embroider the flag of Kosovo for 17 February. Touching each star in turn, she tells Klea about the traditions of each people living in Kosovo and that all should respect each other's cultures. The box names the six communities (Albanians, Serbs, Turks, Bosniaks, Roma, Gorani) and the official languages, Albanian and Serbian.

66.title: Neighbours of Kosovo
66.summary: A map page: pupils name and discuss the neighbouring states that border Kosovo - Serbia, Montenegro, Albania and North Macedonia. The map shows Kosovo with its main cities (Mitrovica, Peja, Prishtina, Ferizaj, Gjakova, Gjilan, Prizren) surrounded by the labelled neighbours.
